extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of public finance, constitutional law, and state government (scholars, policymakers, advanced undergraduates)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository guidance on the principles, problems, and constitutional controls relating to State taxation, types of taxes, exemptions, collection mechanisms, and limits on borrowing and municipal debt. The text surveys practices, defects, and reforms across U.S. States circa late 19th–early 20th century.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property tax and the cardinal rules of taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: "The property tax of to-day, because of its attempt to tax intangible as well as tangible things, sins against the cardinal rules of uniformity, of equality, and of universality of taxation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professor E. R. A. Seligman's statement: taxing intangibles undermines uniformity/equality/universality, puts a premium on dishonesty, debauches the public conscience, presses hardest on those least able to pay, can impose double taxation on one and immunity on another. Use this principle to judge the fairness and practicability of property-tax regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of sworn returns for personal property
rubrics_metrics.description: Oaths and sworn returns as restraints or guarantees of truth have in great measure ceased to be effectual; perjury (direct or constructive) has become so common as to almost cease to occasion notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because sworn declarations often fail, reliance on returns for assessing personal property leads to widespread underreporting and inequity. Policymakers should account for enforcement limits and consider administrative measures beyond oath-taking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of taxing intangible/personal property
rubrics_metrics.description: Large proportions of personal (intangible) property escape taxation; assessors receive few truthful returns and concealment is easier in larger communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical evidence (New York, California, West Virginia, etc.) shows sharp shrinkage of personalty valuations and that personal property contributes a tiny share of state taxation compared with realty. Systems should anticipate concealment strategies and the urban/rich differential in compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions for specified property and persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain descriptions of property commonly exempted: property of the State/local communities, burying grounds, schools/universities, educational/charitable/scientific/literary/agricultural societies, public libraries, churches and religious property, cemeteries, household furniture, farming implements, deposits in savings banks; small personal property below a statutory figure; sometimes ministers have a fixed exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemption lists vary by State; exemptions reduce base and shift burden elsewhere. Designers should list exemptions explicitly and consider effects on equity and revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immunity of federal securities from State taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: No State can tax bonds, debt certificates, or other securities issued by or under the authority of the Federal government (including greenbacks); this doctrine is established by constitutional construction and statute of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This immunity complicates State taxation because taxpayers may convert assets into exempt federal forms to avoid State tax. Tax policy must anticipate such avoidance and the revenue implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of state tax instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: States levy licence/occupation taxes, taxes on corporate franchises, taxes on railroad stock, collateral inheritances; limited use of probate/legacy/succession duties and income tax (nine States authorize it; two permit graduation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of instruments differs widely across States; designers should weigh administrative ease, fairness, and political acceptability. Novel instruments (e.g., stock-exchange transaction taxes) have been used in some States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and application of poll taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Poll taxes are small (typically $1–$3; North Dakota $4); they are sometimes directed to specific uses (schools, poor relief) and occasionally required as a prerequisite to voting (e.g., Tennessee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poll taxes are usually not imposed on women or minors. Consider distributional and civic effects when assigning their uses or conditioning franchise rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential taxation of foreign (out-of-State) corporations
rubrics_metrics.description: "Foreign" corporations (chartered or domiciled in another State) are sometimes taxed more heavily than domestic corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State laws differ widely on corporate taxation; there is a political tendency to target banks and railroads. Expect legal and competitiveness implications when treating foreign vs domestic corporations differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects of licence/occupation taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Licence or occupation taxes are imposed on specific persons/activities: pedlers, hawkers, auctioneers, brokers, pawnbrokers, merchants, commission merchants, 'persons selling by sample,' showmen, jugglers, innkeepers, toll bridges, ferries, telegraphs, express agents, grocery keepers, liquor dealers, insurance vendors of patents, users of franchises, banks, railroads, destructive domestic animals, dealers in options or futures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions and statutes vary in the enumerations; selection reflects social/political judgments about taxable privileges and activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct (state-level) versus local collection of taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some State taxes (licence or corporation taxes) are levied and paid directly to State officials, while the property tax—a major revenue source—is usually collected by local authorities who remit State/county shares as apportioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collection by local authorities saves administrative trouble by consolidating State, county, and municipal levies on one tax-paper, but requires mechanisms for apportionment and equalization among local units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment of State revenue requirements among subunits
rubrics_metrics.description: The State determines needed revenue and apportions it among counties or towns in proportion to their paying capacity (value of property within them); counties likewise apportion between cities and townships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apportionment depends on assessor valuations and boards of equalization; it is central to federated revenue-sharing and affects local tax burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional limits on annual taxation and revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Many States limit by constitution the amount of taxation that may be raised for State purposes in any one year (e.g., Texas originally .5% of valuation, later reduced to .35%; North Dakota .4; Montana .3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some constitutions further direct that no greater revenue be raised than current needs require. Such limits curb reckless expenditure but may cause underfunding of needed services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional restrictions on borrowing by States
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions often restrict State borrowing: requirements for supermajority legislative approval (two-thirds), prohibitions on borrowing for internal improvements, creation of sinking funds to retire debt, and caps on total debt (often small relative to resources).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions were adopted to check past abuses (speculation, jobbery, runaway debt) and include detailed numeric maxima in some States. Exceptions typically exist for military emergency debt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on State aid, credit guarantees, and corporate investments
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Constitutions forbid the legislature to give or lend the credit of the State to any person/association/corporation, to pledge State credit for private liabilities, to take stock in corporations, or otherwise to embark in gainful enterprises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibitions may be absolute or conditional; some allow exceptions by popular vote. They are intended to prevent favoritism, corruption, and loss of public credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on municipal borrowing and debt limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent Constitutions limit borrowing powers of counties/cities/towns (often as a percentage of assessed taxable property — usually 5%, sometimes 7% or 10%) and may restrict the annual tax levy (e.g., one-half percent on valuation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some statutes permit municipalities to exceed limits only by special popular vote (two-thirds, three-fifths, or bare majority of taxpayers). Many require a sinking fund when creating debt. Differences across States are numerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks and evils from unrestricted public enterprise and debt
rubrics_metrics.description: Unrestricted involvement of States or cities in enterprises leads to squandering public domain, enrichment of schemers, corruption of legislation, loss of State credit, great public debts recklessly contracted, wasteful expenditure, embezzlement, public discontent, and financial panic/collapse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical experience motivates constitutional restrictions; policymakers should balance occasional inconvenience of restrictions (piecemeal projects) against the heavy costs of unrestrained public investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergence of progressive inheritance duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Some States have begun to adopt progressive inheritance duties (e.g., Minnesota and Oklahoma authorize it; Oregon enacted an impost reaching 6% for estates exceeding $50,000 in 1909).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inheritance taxation is a developing instrument with varying designs and rates; its adoption reflects shifting fiscal and equity considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergent outcomes: State vs municipal debt trends and causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional safeguards have steadily reduced State debts, whereas municipal indebtedness (especially in large cities) rose sharply; reasons include the ability of States to repudiate/lower debts, later introduction of restrictions on municipalities, lax administration, and opportunities for speculation in city projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistical comparisons (debt totals and per-capita figures across decades) illustrate that institutional design and enforcement determine debt trajectories; reforms should target municipal governance and borrowing controls.
